blocks.text:
A design pattern is a named, proven solution to a problem that keeps coming back. The value is less in the code than in the vocabulary: when a colleague says "wrap it in a decorator" or "make that a builder", both of you instantly picture the same structure. Interviewers use the names for the same reason.

Patterns also age. The classic 1994 book was written for C++ and early Java, and several patterns shrank or vanished when the language gained lambdas, records, enums, sealed types and pattern matching. This Part therefore shows each pattern in the form you would actually write today, and says plainly when the language already does the job.

Creational patterns answer one question: **who creates the object, and how much of the construction does the** **caller need to know?** We cover four: Singleton, Factory, Builder and Prototype.

### Singleton: exactly one instance

**Problem.** Some things should exist once per JVM: a configuration holder, an ID generator, a registry. A global variable would work but gives you no control over creation. A singleton is a class that (1) hides its constructor, (2) creates its single instance itself and (3) hands it out through one access point.

There are three implementations worth knowing. Ranked from best to worst for most code: the enum, the holder idiom, and the eager static field. A fourth, double-checked locking, is mostly of interview interest.

blocks.title: SingletonDemo.java

blocks.code:
$ java SingletonDemo.java
env = dev
same enum instance: true
instances before first use: 0
id 1000
id 1001
instances after: 1
registry broken by reflection: true
enum reflection: IllegalArgumentException: Cannot reflectively create enum objects
blocks.title: Terminal

blocks.text:
#### What to notice

- `enum AppConfig { INSTANCE; }` is the simplest correct singleton. The language guarantees one instance per class loader, and the JVM refuses reflective construction (`Cannot reflectively create enum objects`). Serialization also preserves identity for enums. Effective Java recommends it as the default.
- The holder idiom (`IdGenerator.Holder`) is lazy for free. The nested class `Holder` is not initialized until `getInstance()` first touches it, and class initialization is thread-safe by the JVM specification. The output shows `instances before first use: 0`, proving the laziness.
- A plain `private` constructor is only a convention against reflection: `setAccessible(true)` created a second `Registry`. (On a modular application the module system can block that, but do not rely on it.)

#### Double-checked locking

Before the holder idiom was popular, people wrote lazy singletons with a synchronized check. The correct version needs `volatile`, and it is easy to get wrong:

blocks.title: DoubleChecked.java

blocks.text: Without `volatile`, another thread may see a non-null `instance` whose fields are not yet visible, because the compiler and CPU may reorder the stores inside the constructor with the store to `instance`. Part 8 explains this with the Java memory model (happens-before). The holder idiom gives the same result with no locking code at all, so prefer it.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: Singletons and testing A singleton is global state. Code that calls `AppConfig.INSTANCE` directly is hard to unit test, because you cannot substitute a fake. The usual cure is to create the object once in `main` (or let Spring do it) and pass it to whoever needs it through a constructor. That keeps "one instance" without making every class depend on a global. Spring beans are singletons in exactly this sense: one per application context, but not enforced by the class itself.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How do you make a thread-safe singleton in Java, and which way do you prefer? Enum singleton (`enum X { INSTANCE }`) when no lazy loading is needed, or the initialization-on-demand holder when it is. Both rely on JVM class initialization, which is thread-safe. Double-checked locking works only with a `volatile` field. Mention that reflection can break a plain private constructor and that the enum cannot be broken that way.

### Factory: hide which class gets created

**Problem.** `new Circle(1.5)` ties the caller to a concrete class. If the caller really needs "a shape from this description" or "a notifier for this channel", the choice of class should live in one place that can change.

Three flavours cover almost every real use:

- **Static factory method**: a named `static` method on the class or interface (`List.of`, `Integer.valueOf`, `LocalDate.of`). It can have a descriptive name, return a cached instance, return a subtype and validate. Effective Java makes this the first item.
- **Simple factory**: one method with a `switch` that picks the class from a key, as `of(String kind, ...)` below. With a sealed interface the compiler can also check that you covered every subtype elsewhere.
- **Registry of suppliers**: a `Map<String, Supplier<T>>` so that new kinds can be registered without editing a `switch`. This replaces the heavyweight "Abstract Factory class hierarchy" of the original book.

blocks.title: FactoryDemo.java

blocks.code:
$ java FactoryDemo.java
Circle[r=1.5]                area=7.07
Rect[w=2.0, h=3.0]           area=6.00
Square[side=4.0]             area=16.00
SMS: order shipped
caught: unknown shape: hexagon
[1, 2, 3] 127 2026-10-11
blocks.title: Terminal

blocks.text: The caller sees `Shape` and `Notifier`, never `Circle` or the lambda. Adding a `triangle` means changing the factory only. Adding `push` as a notification channel means adding one map entry.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Pick the lightest form that works If there is one product type and the choice is made once, a static method is enough. Reach for the registry when the set of kinds is open (plugins, configuration-driven choices). Reach for a full factory class hierarchy almost never; if you find yourself writing `AbstractWidgetFactory`, check whether a lambda would do.

### Builder: construct complex objects step by step

**Problem.** A class with many fields, several of them optional, produces either a telescope of constructors (`Order(a)`, `Order(a, b)`, `Order(a, b, c, d)`) or a constructor call full of `null, false, 0`. Nobody can tell what the arguments mean.

A **builder** is a separate mutable object with a method per field and a final `build()`. Calls chain because each setter returns `this`. The finished product can then be immutable, and `build()` is the right place to enforce cross-field rules.

blocks.title: BuilderDemo.java

blocks.code:
$ java BuilderDemo.java
Order[Asha, items=[book, pen], express=true, note=gift wrap]
rejected: at least one item required
rejected: express orders hold at most 3 items
Point[x=1, y=2]
a1true
blocks.title: Terminal

blocks.text:
#### What to notice

- The `Order` constructor is private and takes the builder. The only way to obtain an `Order` is through `build()`, so an invalid order cannot exist.
- `List.copyOf(b.items)` snapshots the list. If the builder were reused afterwards, the already-built order would not change. That is the defensive copy discussed again in the Effective Java chapter.
- The rule "express orders hold at most 3 items" involves two fields, which a setter could not check on its own. `build()` sees them all.
- A `record` with a compact constructor is often all you need for a handful of required fields. Use a builder when there are many optional parameters or when construction has several steps.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: In real code You meet builders constantly: `StringBuilder`, `Stream.builder()`, `HttpRequest.newBuilder()`, `HttpClient.newBuilder()`, Spring's `ResponseEntity.ok().header(...).body(...)`, and Lombok's `@Builder`, which generates the boilerplate shown above. Lombok is an annotation processor and not part of the JDK; many teams use it, others prefer writing builders or using records.

### Prototype: create by copying

**Problem.** Sometimes building an object from scratch is expensive or fiddly, but copying a ready-made one and tweaking it is cheap: a document template, a configured test fixture, a game unit. The **prototype** pattern says: give the object a way to produce a copy of itself.

Java has `Object.clone()` and the `Cloneable` marker interface for this, and both are widely regarded as a design mistake: `clone()` is protected, bypasses constructors, is shallow by default and has a confusing contract. Effective Java advises a **copy constructor** or **copy factory** instead. The program contrasts the options and shows the classic trap of a shallow copy.

blocks.title: PrototypeDemo.java

blocks.code:
$ java PrototypeDemo.java
after shallow edit, base = Report[draft, shared-bug]
base2 = Report[draft]  deep = Report (copy)[draft, v2]
clone() shares the array: a.data[0] = 99
blocks.title: Terminal

blocks.text:
The shallow copy shares the `tags` list with the original, so editing the copy changed `base` too. The copy constructor builds a new `ArrayList`, so the two objects are independent. The same trap exists with `clone()`: it copies the reference to the `int[]`, not the array.

Immutable objects need no prototype at all, because sharing them is safe. Records give you a cheap version of "copy with a change": write a `withTitle(...)` method that calls the canonical constructor.

### Choosing among the four

rows: `enum`, holder class, or a bean created once in `main`/Spring
the class to create depends on input or config
static factory method, `switch` on sealed type, `Map<String, Supplier<T>>`
many optional fields, validation across fields
nested `Builder` class; `record` with compact constructor for small cases
copy constructor or copy factory; avoid `clone()`
blocks.caption: Creational patterns at a glance.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- A pattern is a vocabulary plus a trade-off, not a template to copy; language features have absorbed parts of several of them.
- Singleton: prefer `enum` or the holder idiom; plain private constructors can be bypassed with reflection; DCL needs `volatile`.
- Factory: static factory methods, a switch over a sealed type, or a map of suppliers cover nearly every need.
- Builder: use for many optional parameters and cross-field validation; snapshot mutable inputs in `build()`.
- Prototype: write a copy constructor and copy mutable parts deeply; avoid `clone()`.

Creational patterns decide how objects are born. **Structural patterns** decide how objects and classes are composed into larger structures. **Behavioural patterns** decide how objects divide responsibility and talk to each other. This chapter walks through eleven patterns, each in the form a Java 21 programmer would write, with a complete program you can run.

A recurring theme: since Java 8, many behavioural patterns collapse into "pass a lambda". Since Java 17 to 21, the Visitor pattern collapses into a `switch` over a sealed hierarchy. Knowing the classic shape still matters, because libraries, interviews and legacy code use it.

### Adapter and Decorator

#### Adapter: make an incompatible class fit

**Problem.** You have code that expects interface `Thermometer`, and a third-party `LegacyFahrenheitSensor` you cannot change. An **adapter** implements the interface you want and delegates to the object you have, translating as it goes.

#### Decorator: add behaviour by wrapping

**Problem.** You want to add features (buffering, upper-casing, compression, logging) to an object, in any combination, at run time. Subclassing explodes into `BufferedGzipUpperCaseStream` classes. A **decorator** has the same interface as the thing it wraps, holds a reference to it and adds behaviour before or after delegating. Because the type is unchanged, decorators stack.

The JDK's `java.io` package is the textbook example. `InputStreamReader` is an adapter (bytes to characters). `BufferedReader` and `FilterInputStream` subclasses are decorators. The program builds one of each of our own and then plugs a custom decorator into a real `java.io` chain.

blocks.title: AdapterDecoratorDemo.java

blocks.code: $ java AdapterDecoratorDemo.java body temperature: 37.0 C SALE! SALE! HELLO DECORATORS
blocks.title: Terminal

blocks.text: #### What to notice - `Shout(Bold(Plain(..)))` and `Bold(Shout(Plain(..)))` give different results (`SALE!` versus `SALE!`). Order of wrapping is part of the design; document it. - `UpperCaseInputStream` overrides both `read()` forms of `FilterInputStream`. Forgetting the bulk `read(byte[], int,` `int)` is a classic bug: `BufferedReader` calls the bulk method, so single-byte conversion alone would not have shown. - The chain `BufferedReader(InputStreamReader(UpperCaseInputStream(raw)))` reads inside out: raw bytes, then upper-casing, then charset decoding, then line buffering. The same shape appears with `new` `BufferedOutputStream(new GZIPOutputStream(new FileOutputStream(f)))`.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Adapter versus decorator Both wrap an object. An adapter changes the interface (Fahrenheit sensor becomes `Thermometer`). A decorator keeps the interface and adds behaviour. If a code review asks "which one is this", answer with that sentence.

### Facade and Proxy

#### Facade: one simple door to a complicated subsystem

**Problem.** Placing an order touches inventory, payment and shipping, and every caller must remember the order of calls and the failure handling. A **facade** is a class with a small, task-oriented API (`placeOrder`) that hides the subsystem. It adds no new behaviour; it reduces what callers need to know. Service classes in layered Spring applications often play exactly this role.

#### Proxy: a stand-in that controls access

**Problem.** You want to add access control, lazy loading, caching, logging, retries or transactions around an object without the caller noticing. A **proxy** implements the same interface as the real object and sits in front of it. Unlike a decorator, which is about adding features, a proxy is about controlling access to the target, but in code the two look nearly the same.

Java supports two ways: write the proxy by hand (`CachingRepository`), or generate one at run time with `java.lang.reflect.Proxy`, which creates a class implementing your interfaces and routes every call to one `InvocationHandler`. The second is the foundation of declarative features such as transaction management in Spring (which uses JDK proxies or CGLIB subclassing, depending on the bean).

blocks.title: FacadeProxyDemo.java

blocks.code:
$ java FacadeProxyDemo.java
facade:
  reserve BOOK-1
  charge 12.5
  ship BOOK-1
  result true
caching proxy:
  (cache miss 7)
  row-7
  row-7
dynamic proxy log: [find ok, save failed: empty, caller saw empty]
proxy class is generated: true
blocks.title: Terminal

blocks.text: A few details deserve attention. `method.invoke` wraps any exception thrown by the target in `InvocationTargetException`; the handler unwraps it with `getCause()` and rethrows, so the caller sees the original `IllegalArgumentException` and not a reflection wrapper. A JDK dynamic proxy needs an interface (it cannot proxy a plain class). The caching proxy is not thread safe because it uses a plain `HashMap`; a real one would use `ConcurrentHashMap` or a cache library.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: Where proxies hide in production A Spring `@Transactional` or `@Cacheable` method works because the bean you inject is really a proxy: the proxy opens the transaction, calls your method, then commits or rolls back. This explains the famous gotcha that calling a `@Transactional` method from another method of the same class does nothing special: the call goes `this.method()`, bypassing the proxy.

### Strategy, Observer and Template Method

#### Strategy: pass the algorithm in

**Problem.** A checkout needs a discount rule, and the rules change often (none, 10 percent, flat 15 off). Hard-coding `if` `(type == ...)` chains makes every new rule an edit of a stable class. A **strategy** is an interchangeable algorithm behind a small interface. Since Java 8, any interface with a single abstract method can be implemented with a lambda, so a strategy is usually just a lambda. `Comparator` is the best-known strategy in the JDK: `list.sort(comparator)` receives the ordering algorithm as an argument.

#### Observer: publish/subscribe inside one JVM

**Problem.** One object changes and several others must react, without the subject knowing who they are. The subject keeps a list of listeners and calls them on every change. Swing's `ActionListener`, JavaBeans `PropertyChangeListener` and Spring's `ApplicationEvent` all follow this shape. The old `java.util.Observable` and `Observer` classes were deprecated in Java 9 and should not be used (they are not type safe and `Observable` is a class, not an interface).

#### Template Method: fixed skeleton, variable steps

**Problem.** Several jobs follow the same sequence (load, print header, format rows, print count) and differ in some steps. Put the sequence in a `final` method of an abstract class and let subclasses implement the abstract steps. Servlets (`doGet`), `AbstractList` and JUnit's lifecycle are examples. Composition via Strategy is usually more flexible; use Template Method when the skeleton is truly fixed.

blocks.title: StrategyObserverDemo.java

blocks.code:
$ java StrategyObserverDemo.java
100.0
90.0
85.0
composed: 85.0
display: 101.5
[seen 101.5, seen 102.0]
== report ==
1;Asha
2;Ravi
rows: 2
blocks.title: Terminal

blocks.text:
#### What to notice

- The three discount policies are one-liners. The composed policy uses `andThen`, a hint that strategies built from `Function`-like types combine naturally.
- `subscribe` returns a `Runnable` that unsubscribes, which avoids a separate `unsubscribe(listener)` method. The notify loop iterates over `List.copyOf(listeners)`: without the copy, a listener that unsubscribes itself during a callback would trigger a `ConcurrentModificationException`.
- Observer callbacks run on the publisher's thread, so a slow or throwing listener affects everyone. In production, decide whether to catch exceptions per listener or dispatch asynchronously.
- `run()` is `final` in `ReportJob`: that is what makes it a template and not just an inheritance hook.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: Observer memory leaks A subject holds strong references to its listeners. If a short-lived object subscribes to a long-lived subject and never unsubscribes, it can never be garbage collected. This is one of the classic Java leak patterns (see the memory leak chapter in Part 9). Always provide, and use, an unsubscribe path.

### Command and State

#### Command: a request as an object

**Problem.** You want to queue operations, log them, retry them or undo them. If each action is just a method call, it is gone the moment it returns. A **command** wraps one action and its data in an object with `execute()` (and optionally `undo()`). `Runnable` and `Callable` are commands, and a task submitted to an `ExecutorService` is a command in a queue.

#### State: behaviour depends on the current state

**Problem.** An order can be new, paid or shipped, and the allowed actions differ. Scattering `if (status == PAID)` checks across the code is how invalid transitions sneak in. In the **state** pattern, each state encapsulates its own behaviour and decides the next state. A Java `enum` with abstract methods, as below, is a compact and safe way to write it. The alternative for larger machines is a `Map<State, Set<State>>` of legal transitions.

blocks.title: CommandStateDemo.java

blocks.code:
$ java CommandStateDemo.java
Hello, world
Hello
[]
NEW.ship(): pay first
PAID
SHIPPED
SHIPPED.pay(): already paid
blocks.title: Terminal

blocks.text:
`History` keeps executed commands on a stack, so `undo()` reverses them in last-in first-out order. `Append.undo` works because the command remembers exactly what it appended. For a command whose effect cannot be computed backwards (say "delete line 3"), store a snapshot of the old state in the command.

### Visitor and Iterator

#### Visitor: add operations without touching the classes

**Problem.** You have a family of types (expression nodes) and want many operations over them (evaluate, print, optimise, type-check) without adding a method to every class for each operation. The classic **visitor** uses double dispatch: each node has `accept(Visitor v)`, which calls `v.visitAdd(this)`. It is verbose, and adding a new node type breaks every visitor.

With a `sealed` interface and records (Part 3), the compiler knows the full list of subtypes. A `switch` with record patterns then does the same job with one method per operation, and the compiler reports an error if you forget a case. The cost of the trade is the usual one: it is easy to add operations and hard to add a node type. Visitor with `accept` has the opposite emphasis only slightly; both make "add a node" costly.

blocks.title: VisitorIteratorDemo.java

blocks.code:
$ java VisitorIteratorDemo.java
(2.0 + 3.0 * -4.0) = -10.0
3 2 1 liftoff
blocks.title: Terminal

blocks.text:
#### Iterator: walk without exposing the structure

**Problem.** Callers should traverse a collection (list, tree, database cursor) without knowing how it stores its data. Java built this into the language: any class implementing `Iterable<T>` works in an enhanced `for` loop, as `Countdown` does above. `hasNext()` and `next()` are the whole contract. `Iterator.remove()` is optional. Most collection iterators are **fail-fast**: modifying the collection during iteration, other than through the iterator, throws `ConcurrentModificationException` (the details are in Part 6).

### Patterns in the JDK: a reading list

headers: In the JDK or common libraries
blocks.caption: Where to see each pattern in code you already use.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Which design patterns have you used, and where? Pick three you can defend with a concrete case: for example Strategy for pluggable discount or sorting rules (a `Comparator` or lambda), Builder for a request object with many optional parts, and Proxy via Spring's `@Transactional`. For each, state the problem, the structure in one sentence, and the trade-off (indirection, extra classes, harder debugging). Interviewers care that you chose a pattern because of a problem, not the other way round.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Adapter changes an interface, Decorator adds behaviour behind the same interface, Proxy controls access, Facade simplifies a subsystem.
- Strategy and Command are usually lambdas in modern Java; Observer needs an unsubscribe path to avoid leaks.
- Template Method fixes the skeleton in a `final` method; prefer composition when the skeleton is not truly fixed.
- State fits naturally in an `enum` with abstract methods; Visitor becomes a `switch` over a sealed hierarchy with exhaustiveness checking.
- `java.io` and `java.lang.reflect.Proxy` are the JDK's best examples of Decorator, Adapter and Proxy.

Design patterns tell you how to arrange classes. This chapter is about something smaller and more frequent: the habits that separate code that merely works from code that stays correct as it grows. The best-known collection of these habits is *Effective Java* by Joshua Bloch, who designed much of `java.util` and the Java collections. Its 90 or so "items" are rules of thumb backed by real failures. We do not reproduce the book; we pick the dozen items that matter most to a working engineer and demonstrate each with code you can run. Where a rule has a reason, the reason is given, because a rule you understand can be applied to cases the book never mentioned.

The theme of nearly every item is the same: **make misuse impossible, or at least obvious**. Do it with types (enums, records, `Optional`), with immutability, and with small public surfaces.

### Creating objects

#### Prefer static factories and builders

Covered in the creational patterns chapter, so only the summary. Use a static factory (`Money.ofCents(250)`) when a name or caching helps, and a builder when there are many optional parameters. Both let you keep the real constructor `private`, which leaves the class free to change how objects are made later. A public constructor is a promise you can never take back.

#### Prefer dependency injection to hard-wired resources

A class that does `new DatabaseConnection("prod-host")` inside its methods cannot be tested without a database. Accept the collaborator through the constructor instead. The clean code chapter that follows shows this step by step.

#### Avoid creating needless objects

`new String("hello")` creates a second object where the literal `"hello"` is already shared; `Boolean.valueOf(true)` reuses an instance while `new Boolean(true)` (deprecated for removal) does not. A subtler version: `Long sum = 0L;` `sum += i;` inside a loop allocates a new `Long` on every iteration (the performance chapter at the end of this Part measures it). The balance matters: do not contort code to save objects that the JIT will remove anyway (see escape analysis in Part 9). Reuse expensive objects (a compiled `Pattern`, a `DateTimeFormatter`, an `ObjectMapper`) by putting them in a `static final` field.

### Immutability and defensive copies

An **immutable** class is one whose instances cannot change after construction (`String`, `Integer`, `LocalDate`, records of immutables). Immutable objects are thread-safe without locks, safe to share and cache, safe as `HashMap` keys, and trivial to reason about. Bloch's advice: *classes should be immutable unless there is a very good reason to make them* *mutable.* The recipe:

1. No setters or other methods that change state.
2. Make the class `final` (or make all constructors private), so a subclass cannot add mutable behaviour.
3. Make all fields `private final`.
4. Copy any mutable object that comes in through the constructor, and never hand out the internal mutable object.

Step 4 is where most mistakes hide, because `final` only protects the *reference*, not the object it points to. The next listing shows the attack in `BrokenPeriod`, and the cure.

blocks.title: Effective.java

blocks.code:
$ java Effective.java
end changed: true
end now: -5
2026-05-02 after 2026-05-01
[Asha, Ravi] vs [Asha, Ravi, Mallory]
immutable view
$12.50 true
true APPLE 1
ASHA@EXAMPLE.COM
none
addCount = 6
blocks.title: Run it (Java 21)

blocks.text:
`Date` is used here only to demonstrate the attack; the chapter on date and time in Part 4 explains why `java.time` replaced it.

**What to notice.** `BrokenPeriod` looks immutable: both fields are `private final`. Yet `end.setTime(0)`, called on the original `Date` the caller still holds, changed the period, and `p.end().setTime(-5)` changed it through the accessor. Output lines 1 and 2 prove it. There are two fixes: copy on the way in and out (`new Date(start.getTime())`), or, better, use a type that is itself immutable. `java.time.LocalDate` is immutable, which is why the `Period` record needs only a validation check in its compact constructor and no copying at all. Choose immutable field types and the problem disappears.

The `Roster`/`LeakyRoster` pair shows the same bug with collections. `LeakyRoster` kept the caller's list, so `Mallory` appeared later in a roster that "never changes". `Roster` takes a snapshot with `List.copyOf` and exposes an immutable list, so any attempt to modify it throws `UnsupportedOperationException`. Note the order of the checks: when you copy a mutable parameter, **copy first, then validate the copy**; otherwise another thread can change the original between the check and the copy (a time-of-check to time-of-use race).

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Records are shallow. A record's fields are `final`, but `record Team(List<String> members)` still shares whatever list it is given. Use the compact constructor to copy: `members = List.copyOf(members);`. The records chapter in Part 3 covers this.

### Methods every class gets: equals, hashCode, toString

The `equals` contract (reflexive, symmetric, transitive, consistent, never equal to `null`) and the rule *equal objects must* *have equal hash codes* were demonstrated in the chapter on the `Object` class in Part 3. The practical advice here is how to avoid hand-writing them:

- For a value type, **use a** `record`: `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString` are generated from all components and are correct by construction.
- If you must write them, use `Objects.equals(a, b)` and `Objects.hash(a, b, c)`, and compare exactly the fields that define identity.
- If you override `equals`, always override `hashCode`; breaking this makes `HashMap` and `HashSet` lose your objects.
- Always override `toString` on any class whose objects appear in logs. Include the fields useful for debugging, but never secrets (see the secure coding chapter).
- Never put mutable fields in `hashCode` of an object used as a map key. Mutating the object after insertion strands it in the wrong bucket.

Implement `Comparable` when a type has a natural order, and keep it consistent with `equals` (`compareTo` returning 0 should mean `equals` is true), or sorted collections and hash collections will disagree about duplicates. Compare primitives with `Integer.compare`, not by subtracting, which overflows.

### Classes and inheritance

#### Favour composition over inheritance

Inheritance couples a subclass to the *implementation* of its superclass, not just its interface. The last block in the listing is Bloch's famous example. `InstrumentedSet` extends `HashSet` to count how many elements were added. We add three elements with `addAll` and expect `addCount` to be 3. It is **6**. The reason is hidden in `HashSet`'s implementation: `addAll` internally calls `add` for each element, so each element is counted twice, once in our `addAll` and once in our overridden `add`. A later JDK version could change `addAll` to not call `add`, and our class would silently change behaviour again.

The fix is **composition with forwarding**: hold a `Set` in a private field, implement the `Set` interface by forwarding each method to it, and add the counting in your own methods. Then you depend on the *contract* of `Set`, not on how `HashSet` happens to be written. Inheritance is appropriate when the subclass truly *is a* kind of the superclass, both are under your control, and the superclass was designed and documented for extension. Otherwise either make the class `final`, or forbid overriding by making methods `final`.

#### Minimise accessibility

Make every class and member as inaccessible as it can be: `private` by default, package-private next, `public` only for the real API. In a module (Part 11) export only the packages that form the API. Public fields are almost always wrong (except `public static final` constants of immutable type), because you can never validate or change them. Keep a class's public surface small: each public method is a commitment.

#### Use interfaces to define types; prefer them as parameter and return types

Declare `List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();` and write methods that accept `Collection<String>` or `List<String>` rather than `ArrayList<String>`. Callers keep their freedom, and you can change the implementation. Use `Set`, `Map` and `Queue` the same way.

### Enums, not integer constants

Before Java 5 programmers wrote `static final int APPLE = 0, ORANGE = 1;`. Nothing stops `eat(42)`, printing shows `0`, and a name cannot be recovered. In the listing the `Fruit` enum fixes all of this: it is type-safe (a method taking a `Fruit` cannot be passed `42`), prints as `APPLE`, can carry fields and methods (Part 3, chapter on enums), works in `switch` with exhaustiveness checking, and has fast specialised collections `EnumMap` and `EnumSet`. Use enums for any fixed set known at compile time: days, states, roles, operations. Two warnings: never rely on `ordinal()` for anything persisted (reordering the constants silently changes it), and never use bit-field integer flags where an `EnumSet` expresses the same thing readably.

### Generics and collections

- **Do not use raw types.** `List list = new ArrayList();` throws away compile-time checking and moves `ClassCastException` to run time. Use `List<String>`, or `List<?>` when you truly do not care.
- **Prefer lists to arrays** when combining with generics. Arrays are covariant and reified (`String[]` is a subtype of `Object[]`, and the store check happens at run time); generics are invariant and erased. Mixing them gives warnings for good reason.
- **Use bounded wildcards for flexibility: PECS.** *Producer extends, Consumer super.* A method that only reads items out of a collection takes `Collection<? extends E>`; one that only puts items in takes `Collection<? super` `E>`. This is why `Collections.copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src)` has that signature (see the wildcard chapter in Part 6).
- **Eliminate unchecked warnings** or, when you can prove safety, suppress the narrowest scope possible with `@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")` plus a comment explaining why it is safe.
- **Return empty collections, never** `null`**.** `Collections.emptyList()` or `List.of()` costs nothing and saves every caller a `null` check.

### Methods

#### Check parameters for validity, early, and document it

Validate arguments at the top of public methods and fail with a clear message: `Objects.requireNonNull(name,` `"name")`, `if (qty <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("qty must be positive: " + qty)`. Failing fast puts the stack trace at the real cause. For private methods use `assert`.

#### Design signatures carefully

Choose names that follow convention, avoid long parameter lists (more than about four: introduce a parameter object, a record, or a builder), and prefer two-element enums to `boolean` parameters when the call site would be unreadable (`render(true, false)` versus `render(Mode.DRAFT, Colour.MONO)`). Avoid overloads with the same number of parameters in the same position, and especially ones that differ only by a boxed/primitive pair (`remove(int)` versus `remove(Object)` on `List` is the famous trap).

#### Return `Optional` for "might be absent", not `null`

`Optional<T>` as a *return type* tells the caller in the signature that there may be no result, and its methods (`map`, `orElse`, `ifPresent`) make handling it fluent, as `findEmail` does in the listing: `ASHA@EXAMPLE.COM` for a known user, `none` for an unknown one. Use it only for return values. Do not use `Optional` for fields, method parameters or collection elements (it adds an object and noise without benefit), never call `get()` without checking `isPresent()` (prefer `orElseThrow()`), and never return `null` from a method whose type is `Optional`. For collections and arrays return an empty one.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: `Optional.of(null)` throws. `Optional.of(x)` requires a non-null `x` and throws `NullPointerException` otherwise. Use `Optional.ofNullable(x)` when `x` may be null. Passing a possibly-null value to `of` is a common beginner bug.

### Exceptions

Part 5 covers the mechanics. The Effective Java advice, in one list:

- Use exceptions only for exceptional conditions, never for ordinary control flow (such as ending a loop by catching `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`).
- Use **checked** exceptions for conditions a caller can reasonably recover from, and **unchecked** (`RuntimeException`) for programming errors such as a violated precondition. Many modern codebases lean to unchecked exceptions everywhere, since checked ones do not compose well with lambdas.
- Prefer the standard exceptions: `IllegalArgumentException`, `IllegalStateException`, `NullPointerException`, `IndexOutOfBoundsException`, `UnsupportedOperationException`, `ConcurrentModificationException`. Readers already know what they mean.
- Throw exceptions that fit the abstraction level and keep the cause: `throw new OrderException("cannot load` `order 7", sqlException);`. Never swallow an exception with an empty `catch` block; if you really mean to ignore it, name the variable `ignored` and say why in a comment.
- Include the values that caused the failure in the message (`"qty must be positive: -3"`), but not secrets.
- Use try-with-resources for anything `AutoCloseable`; it closes in reverse order and records secondary failures as suppressed exceptions instead of losing them.

### Other items worth knowing

#### Use `@Override` always

It turns a typo (`equals(Foo f)` instead of `equals(Object o)`, which overloads instead of overriding) into a compile error.

#### Prefer the standard library

Do not write your own random number code, sort, or `Pair`; use `ThreadLocalRandom`, `List.sort`, a record. The JDK is better tested and your readers know it.

#### Beware of `float` and `double` for money

They cannot represent 0.1 exactly. Use `BigDecimal`, or store integer cents as the `Money` class in the listing does (Part 4 shows why).

#### Prefer `for-each` loops and `StringBuilder`

The enhanced `for` loop avoids index and iterator bugs. Use `StringBuilder` for repeated appends in loops.

#### Do not use finalizers or `Cleaner` for resources

Finalization is deprecated for removal. Release resources with `AutoCloseable` and try-with-resources (Part 9 has the details).

### Evolving an API without breaking users

A public API ages. Code written against version 1 must keep compiling and running against version 2, and the longer a library lives the more careful it must be. These rules apply to any shared library or internal module with many callers.

- **Never remove or change a public method in a way that breaks callers.** Instead add a new method and mark the old one `@Deprecated(since = "2.0", forRemoval = false)` with a Javadoc `@deprecated` tag pointing to the replacement. Use `forRemoval = true` only when you really plan to delete it; the compiler then emits a stronger warning, as it does for `Thread.stop`.
- **Adding a method to an interface** breaks every implementor unless you give it a `default` implementation. That is the reason `default` methods exist (they let `List.sort` and `Collection.stream` be added in Java 8 without breaking decade-old implementations).
- **Adding a component to a record** changes its canonical constructor, which breaks callers. Keep an old constructor delegating to the new one.
- **Distinguish source from binary compatibility.** Changing a method's return type or making a parameter type more general can still compile but breaks already compiled callers, which look methods up by the exact descriptor (see the class file chapter in Part 1). Tools such as `japicmp` check this in a build.
- **Seal or hide what you may want to change.** Final classes, package-private helpers and unexported module packages cannot be depended on, so you can change them freely. A sealed interface lets you add subtypes without outside implementors existing.
- **Document the contract**, including thread safety, null handling and exceptions, with Javadoc, and follow *semantic* *versioning* (major.minor.patch) so users know what an upgrade may break.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Why is composition preferred over inheritance? Give an example. Inheritance exposes a subclass to the superclass's implementation details, so a change in the parent, or a self-call inside it, can break the child, and it ties the child to one parent for life. Composition holds the other object in a field and delegates, so you depend only on its public contract, can swap it, and can combine several. Example: a counting `HashSet` subclass reports 6 after `addAll` of 3 elements because `HashSet.addAll` calls `add`; a wrapper that holds a `Set` and forwards counts correctly.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How do you make a class immutable? Make it final (or have private constructors), make all fields private and final, provide no mutators, copy mutable inputs in the constructor and mutable outputs in accessors (or hold immutable types such as `List.copyOf`, `LocalDate`), and do not let `this` escape during construction. A record is a shortcut, but remember it is shallow for mutable components.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: In Spring Boot code, DTOs are increasingly records, entities keep a no-argument constructor because the persistence framework needs it, and services are immutable objects with `final` fields set by constructor injection. Following the items above, `final` fields plus constructor injection, is what makes a Spring bean easy to test without starting any framework.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Effective Java boils down to making wrong code hard to write.

- Prefer immutability: `private final` fields, no setters, copy mutable inputs and outputs, or choose immutable field types such as `LocalDate` and `List.copyOf`.
- Prefer composition and interfaces to inheritance; a subclass depends on how its parent is implemented, and the counting-set example shows how that goes wrong.
- Use enums instead of int constants, `Optional` as a return type for absence, empty collections instead of `null`, and standard exceptions with clear messages and causes.
- Validate arguments early, avoid raw types, apply PECS to wildcards, and override `equals` and `hashCode` together, or use a record.
- Evolve APIs by adding and deprecating, not by changing or removing; use `default` methods to extend interfaces.

sections.title: Clean code and code smells in Java

blocks.text:
Code is read far more often than it is written: by teammates, by reviewers, and by you six months from now. "Clean code" is simply code that a competent stranger can understand and change safely. This chapter turns that vague goal into specific habits: how to name things, how big a method should be, the design principles known as SOLID applied to small Java examples, a catalogue of **code smells** (surface signs that the design underneath is in trouble), a worked before/after refactoring that you can run, and **dependency injection by hand**, the one technique that makes the rest testable.

None of this is law. They are heuristics that experienced developers converge on, and each has exceptions. Learn them as questions to ask of your code, not as rules to follow blindly.

### Naming

A good name removes the need for a comment. Names are the cheapest and most powerful tool you have.

- **Say what, not how.** `calculateTax(order)` over `doStuff(o)`. A reader should be able to guess what a method does from its call site.
- **Be consistent with Java conventions.** Classes and records `UpperCamelCase` nouns (`OrderService`); methods and variables `lowerCamelCase` (verbs for methods: `findByEmail`, `isEmpty`, `hasNext`); constants `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE`; packages all lower case. Booleans read as questions: `active`, `isExpired()`, `canRetry()`.
- **Length proportional to scope.** `i` in a three-line loop is fine; a field used across a 500-line class deserves a full name. Avoid abbreviations nobody else would guess (`cstmrLst`).
- **No noise words.** `OrderData`, `OrderInfo`, `OrderObject` add nothing over `Order`. Do not encode the type: `nameString`, `ListOfUsers`.
- **One word per concept.** If you call fetching `get` in one class, `fetch` in another and `retrieve` in a third, the reader wonders what the difference is. Pick one.
- **Use domain words.** If the business says "invoice", the class is `Invoice`, not `BillingDocument`.

### Methods and classes: small, focused, at one level

**A method should do one thing, and do it at one level of abstraction.** A useful test: can you describe what the method does in one sentence without using "and"? A method that parses input, validates it, computes a price and writes a file does four things, and any change to one risks the other three. Typical guidelines: a method that does not fit on one screen (say 20 to 30 lines) deserves a look; more than three or four parameters suggest a missing object; a flag parameter (`process(order, true)`) means the method does two things and should be split in two.

**Nesting is a smell.** Deeply nested `if`s hide the main path. Use **guard clauses** to handle the odd cases first and return early:

blocks.title: (fragment)

blocks.text:
**Comments explain why, not what.** `// increment i` is noise. `// the API returns 1-based pages, we use` `0-based` explains a decision the code cannot show. If you feel the need to write a comment explaining a block, first try extracting the block into a method whose name says the same thing. Javadoc on public API is different: document the contract.

**Classes should be cohesive.** All the fields should be used by most of the methods. A class with two groups of fields each used by separate groups of methods is two classes. A good class can be described in one sentence.

### SOLID, with small examples

SOLID is a set of five object-oriented design principles. Each one is short; the skill is spotting when your code violates it.

#### S: Single Responsibility Principle

*A class should have one reason to change.* An `OrderService` that calculates prices, saves to the database, formats e-mails and prints PDFs changes whenever pricing, storage, wording or layout changes. Split by responsibility: `PriceCalculator`, `OrderRepository`, `ReceiptFormatter`. Each can then be tested alone, and a change in e-mail wording cannot break pricing.

#### O: Open/Closed Principle

*Open for extension, closed for modification.* Adding a new kind of discount should not mean editing a growing `if/else` chain in a pricing method. Put the varying part behind an interface (strategy pattern) and add a new implementation. Enums with per-constant behaviour, and sealed interfaces with a pattern `switch`, are lighter-weight ways to reach the same goal. The refactoring below does exactly this.

#### L: Liskov Substitution Principle

*A subtype must be usable wherever its supertype is expected, without surprises.* The classic violation: `Square extends` `Rectangle` with `setWidth` that also changes height. Code that sets width and height independently and then computes the area gets the wrong answer when handed a `Square`. In Java terms, an overriding method must accept at least what the parent accepts, promise at least what it promises, and not throw new unexpected exceptions. If you find yourself overriding a method to throw `UnsupportedOperationException`, the inheritance is probably wrong (the JDK's own `Collections.unmodifiableList` and `List.of` are a known compromise, which is why `List.add` is documented as optional).

#### I: Interface Segregation Principle

*Do not force clients to depend on methods they do not use.* One fat `Worker` interface with `work()`, `eat()` and `sleep()` forces a robot class to implement `eat()`. Split it into small role interfaces. The JDK follows this: `Iterable`, `Comparable`, `Closeable` and `Runnable` are one-method roles that classes combine freely.

#### D: Dependency Inversion Principle

*High-level code should depend on abstractions, not on concrete low-level classes.* A `WelcomeService` should know that it can "notify someone", not that it sends mail through a specific SMTP library. Define a `Notifier` interface owned by the high-level code, and let the concrete class implement it. The mechanism that wires the concrete choice in is dependency injection, below.

### A catalogue of code smells

A **code smell** does not mean the code is wrong; it means look closer. The most common ones in Java, each with the usual cure:

rows: one method of 80 lines with comments marking "sections"
extract method (each section becomes a named method)
`createUser(a, b, c, d, e, f, g)`
the same five lines pasted in three classes
method uses another object's getters more than its own fields
move the method to that object
3000 lines, 60 fields, "Manager" or "Util" in its name
`if (x instanceof A) ... else if (x` `instanceof B)` repeated
polymorphism, or sealed type with pattern `switch`
handle, rethrow with cause, or log with context
tell, don't ask; add a method on `a`

blocks.text:
### Worked refactoring: before and after

The listing shows one realistic small method, written the way it often arrives in a pull request, and a cleaned version with identical behaviour. Both are in one file, so the output proves they agree. The second half of the file is dependency injection, explained after it.

blocks.title: Refactor.java

blocks.code:
$ java Refactor.java
before: 141.75
after:  141.75
MAIL to asha@example.com: Welcome, asha
true
false []
true [asha@example.com|Welcome, asha]
blocks.title: Run it (Java 21)

blocks.text:
Both versions print `141.75` (two items of 100 and 50 with 5% food tax is 157.5, then 10% off for VIP). Now compare how each reads.

#### What was wrong with the before version

Every one-letter name (`o`, `t`, `i`, `p`) forces you to decode. The input is a `List<String[]>` of "name, price" pairs, a stringly-typed structure whose meaning lives only in the author's head (primitive obsession). The boolean `vip` and the string `type` are flag arguments: a typo such as `"Food"` silently takes the 20% branch. The numbers `1.05`, `1.2` and `0.9` are magic. The method parses, validates, taxes and discounts, four jobs in one, with four levels of nesting. Adding a third category or discount means editing the middle of it, an Open/Closed violation, and testing the discount logic means constructing string arrays.

#### What the after version does

- `Item` is a record: the data has a name and type. Parsing strings becomes the job of the layer that reads input, not of the pricing code.
- `Category` is an enum that owns its tax rate. A new category is one new constant, a typo is a compile error, and the arithmetic lives next to the data it uses. The `switch` on a string is gone.
- `Discount` is a one-method interface (a strategy), so `NONE` and `VIP` are lambdas, and a new discount is a new lambda. The `total` method has no flag.
- `total` itself is two lines at one level of abstraction: add up taxed prices, then apply the discount.

Behaviour is identical, but the new code is split into pieces that can each be understood and tested alone. Note also what we did **not** do: no `AbstractPricingStrategyFactory`. The cure for a smell should be smaller than the smell.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Never refactor without a safety net. A refactoring changes structure but not behaviour, and you can only claim that if something checks it. Write or run tests first (the testing chapter in Part 11 shows how), change in small steps, and run the tests after each step. In the listing, `main` itself acts as the net: both versions must print the same number.

### Dependency injection by hand

A class that creates its own collaborators is welded to them. If `WelcomeService` did `new SmtpNotifier("mail.corp")` internally, you could not run it without a mail server, and every test would send e-mail. **Dependency injection** (DI) inverts this: the class declares what it needs, as constructor parameters of interface type, and whoever builds the object decides which concrete implementations to supply.

In the second half of `Refactor.java` there is no framework. `WelcomeService` takes a `UserRepo` and a `Notifier`, both interfaces. In `main`, "production" wiring passes a console notifier, and "test" wiring passes a fake notifier that records messages into a list. The test asserts on that list: `true [asha@example.com|Welcome, asha]` shows the right message went to the right address, and `false []` shows an unknown user sends nothing. No mail server, no database, no framework, just constructors.

Three reasons to prefer **constructor injection** over field or setter injection:

- Dependencies are `final`, so the object is never half-built.
- The constructor makes the dependencies visible. A constructor with eight parameters is the class telling you it violates single responsibility.
- The class can be created in a plain unit test with `new`.

#### The composition root

All the wiring should happen in one place near the program's entry point, often called the **composition root**: `main` creates the repository, the notifier and the services and connects them. Nothing else in the code base calls `new` on a service. A DI container such as Spring does the same job with annotations: `@Component` and `@Service` mark the classes, constructor parameters declare the needs, and the container acts as an automated composition root. Understanding the manual version first means Spring's `@Autowired` is no longer magic, just a machine that calls your constructors in the right order.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: In a Spring Boot service the layering is almost always `Controller` (HTTP) calls `Service` (rules) calls `Repository` (database), each depending on the next through an interface and constructor injection. A unit test for the service builds it with `new`, passing a mock or fake repository (Mockito generates such fakes). Tests that need the whole container are slower and used sparingly.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What are the SOLID principles? Give one example violation. Single responsibility (one reason to change), open/closed (extend without modifying), Liskov substitution (subtypes honour the parent's contract), interface segregation (small client-specific interfaces), dependency inversion (depend on abstractions). Example: `Square extends Rectangle` where `setWidth` also sets the height violates Liskov, because code written for rectangles breaks when given a square. Another: a `ReportService` with an `if (type.equals("pdf")) ... else if (type.equals("csv"))` chain violates open/closed; each new format edits the method, while with a `Formatter` interface it is a new class.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What is the difference between dependency injection and dependency inversion? Dependency inversion is the design principle: high-level modules and low-level modules both depend on abstractions, and the abstraction is owned by the high-level side. Dependency injection is a technique to achieve it: objects receive their dependencies from outside (usually through the constructor) instead of creating them. Inversion of control is the broader idea, that a framework or caller controls object creation and flow rather than your code.

### A habit to take away: the review checklist

Before you push code, read your own diff as a reviewer would, with these questions: Could a new teammate name what each method does from its name alone? Is anything duplicated? Is there a method I would have to scroll to read? Does any class have two reasons to change? Is every value that could be wrong (null, negative, empty) checked where it enters? Can I test this with plain `new`? Is there a comment explaining *what* the code does that a better name would make unnecessary? One or two "no" answers per change is normal; the habit is to notice them.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Clean code is code that is cheap to change safely.

- Choose names from the domain, keep methods small and at one level of abstraction, flatten nesting with guard clauses, and comment the why.
- SOLID in one line each: one reason to change; extend without editing; subtypes honour contracts; small interfaces; depend on abstractions.
- Learn the smell catalogue (long method, primitive obsession, flag arguments, god class, feature envy, switch on type), and cure each with the smallest refactoring that works.
- Refactor only under test, in small steps.
- Inject dependencies through constructors, wire everything in one composition root, and your classes become testable with plain `new`.

Security is not a feature you add at the end; it is a property of how every line handles data it did not create. Most real-world breaches of Java services are not exotic cryptographic attacks. They are old, boring bugs: a string pasted into a SQL query, a file path taken from a request, an object deserialized from the network, a password in a log file, a library with a known hole that nobody upgraded. This chapter covers those, because they account for most of the damage and because each has a small, specific habit that prevents it.

Java gives you a head start: no buffer overflows or dangling pointers (the JVM checks array bounds and manages memory), and a strong standard library. It does not protect you from trusting the wrong input. The central mindset is therefore one sentence: **treat all data that crosses a trust boundary as hostile until validated**. Trust boundaries are the HTTP request, the file you read, the message from a queue, the environment variable, the response from another service, and the bytes of a serialized object.

### Input validation: allow-lists, at the boundary

**Problem.** Code downstream assumes its inputs are sane: that a username has no quotes, a quantity is positive, a name is not 10 MB long. If the assumption is false, something breaks, sometimes something exploitable.

**Idea.** Validate at the boundary, where untrusted data enters, and validate against what is *allowed*, not against what is known to be bad. A **deny-list** ("reject input containing `DROP`") is endlessly bypassable: `dRoP`, comment tricks, encodings. An **allow-list** ("a username is 3 to 16 letters, digits or underscores") is short and complete. In the listing below, `validateUsername` is exactly that, and the result shows `a; DROP` rejected without any attempt to recognise attacks.

Practical rules:

- Check **type, length, range and format**, in that order. Reject, do not silently "fix" input.
- Convert strings to real types as early as possible (`int`, `UUID`, enum, `LocalDate`, a record such as `Email`). A parsed `UUID` cannot contain a quote.
- Cap sizes: maximum request body, maximum string length, maximum collection size, maximum nesting. Unbounded input is a denial-of-service vector.
- **Canonicalise before you check**: decode and normalise (Unicode `Normalizer`, `Path.normalize()`), then validate the canonical form. Checking first and decoding later is a classic bypass.
- Validation is not escaping. Validating that input "looks fine" does not make it safe to paste into SQL, HTML or a shell command. Each destination needs its own safe mechanism (below).
- Frameworks help: Bean Validation (`@NotNull`, `@Size`, `@Pattern`) in Spring Boot declares these rules on request objects. They still need to be applied on every endpoint.

Beware your own regular expressions: a pattern with nested quantifiers such as `(a+)+$` can take exponential time on crafted input (see the regex chapter in Part 4). Keep patterns simple and bounded, which also helps here since `{3,16}` caps the length.

### Injection: never build commands out of strings

**Injection** is the family of attacks in which data is interpreted as code. SQL injection is the famous one, but the same bug exists for operating-system commands, LDAP queries, JNDI lookups and HTML (cross-site scripting).

#### SQL injection and the PreparedStatement

Look at what string concatenation produces. In the listing the user name is `x' OR '1'='1`, and the query built by `+` comes out as:

blocks.code: SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = 'x' OR '1'='1'

blocks.text: The quote in the data ended the string literal, and the rest became part of the SQL: the condition is now always true and every row matches. With a semicolon the attacker could also append a second statement. The fix is **parameterised queries**: the SQL text and the values travel separately, and the database driver treats the value strictly as data, whatever characters it contains.

blocks.title: (fragment, needs a database to run)

blocks.text: Rules that follow: always use `PreparedStatement` (or the equivalent in your framework: Spring Data's derived queries, JPA's named parameters `:name`, `JdbcTemplate` with `?`); never concatenate or `String.format` values into SQL; and remember that **placeholders only stand for values**, not for table names, column names or `ORDER BY` directions. If those must vary, choose them from a fixed allow-list (an enum or a `Map`) in your own code, never from raw input. JDBC itself is outside the scope of this book, but this habit is not.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: ORMs do not make you immune. JPA/Hibernate protects you only when you use parameters. A JPQL string built by concatenation (`"from User where name = '" + n + "'"`) is just as injectable as raw SQL. The same holds for `@Query` strings and native queries.

#### Command injection

`Runtime.exec("convert " + filename)` is the same bug for the shell. Use `ProcessBuilder` with a list of arguments, which never goes through a shell: `new ProcessBuilder("convert", filename, "out.png")`. Even so, a value starting with `-` can be read as an option by the program, so validate it first or place it after `--` where the tool supports that. If you can avoid starting a process at all (use a library), do.

#### Output encoding

When data goes into HTML, escape it for HTML; into JSON, use a JSON library rather than concatenation; into a log line, strip newlines (log injection lets an attacker forge entries). Template engines such as Thymeleaf escape by default; turning that off is a decision to review.

### Path traversal

**Problem.** A download endpoint takes `?file=report.pdf` and opens `uploads/` plus that name. An attacker sends `../../etc/passwd` and reads files outside the folder. This is **path traversal**.

**Fix.** Resolve the user-supplied part against the base directory, normalise, and check the result still starts with the base. The helper `resolveSafe` in the listing does that, and the output shows each case.

The interesting part is the last pair of lines of the first block: `base.resolve("../../etc/passwd").normalize()` gives `/srv/etc/passwd`, a path outside `/srv/app/uploads`, which is what the `startsWith` check catches. Three details matter:

- `Path.normalize()` removes `.` and `..` segments **lexically**, without touching the file system. It does not resolve symbolic links. If users can create symlinks inside the base directory, additionally compare `toRealPath()` results.
- `Path.resolve(other)` returns `other` unchanged when it is absolute. That is why `"/etc/passwd"` is also rejected: resolving it against the base yields `/etc/passwd`, which fails the check.
- `Path.startsWith(Path)` compares **path elements**, not characters. `Path.of("/srv/up2/f").startsWith("/srv/up")` is `false`, whereas a plain string `startsWith` would wrongly say true. Always use the `Path` method, never `toString().startsWith`.

Also never trust a client-supplied file *name* for the saved name: generate your own (a `UUID`), and keep the original only as metadata. Check the real content type, not just the extension, and cap the size.

### Deserialization

Java's built-in serialization (Part 5) rebuilds objects from a byte stream by choosing classes named *inside the stream*, and runs their `readObject` code while doing so. If an attacker controls the bytes, and a class on your class path has a "gadget" (code that does something dangerous when deserialized, such as running a command through a chain of method calls), they can execute code on your server before your `readObject` call even returns. Libraries such as Apache Commons Collections have been the source of many such chains, and this has been behind remote-code-execution bugs in many well-known Java products.

The rules, in order of strength:

1. **Never deserialize untrusted data with** `ObjectInputStream`**.** Use a data format instead: JSON (Jackson, Gson), Protocol Buffers, or plain text. These do not name arbitrary classes in the stream.
2. If you must, install a **deserialization filter** (JEP 290, Java 9, backported; context-specific filters from Java 17 on). A filter is an allow-list of classes, plus limits on depth and size, checked *before* each class is instantiated.
3. Remember that a JSON library can also be configured dangerously: enabling polymorphic "default typing" on Jackson recreates the same problem in JSON form. Bind to concrete, known types.
4. Records and sealed hierarchies deserialized through a JSON binding are safer than `Serializable` classes, but still validate the values.

The listing shows rule 2 in about ten lines. The filter `java.lang.Integer;java.lang.Number;java.lang.Object;java.util.ArrayList;!*` means: allow these four, reject everything else (`!*`). An `ArrayList` of integers is accepted and prints `[1, 2]`; a `HashSet` is rejected with `InvalidClassException: filter status: REJECTED` before any of its code runs. Why do `Number` and `Object` appear? Because `Integer` extends `Number`, the stream describes the superclass as well, and an `ArrayList` is stored internally with an `Object[]` array, and the filter sees each of those. Finding the minimal allow-list is trial and error, which is a good indication of how much code runs during deserialization.
